blogs.title: Beyond the Triad: Recognizing Telomere Biology Disorders When Dyskeratosis Congenita's Classic Features Are Absent
blogs.description: This post explores the diagnostic challenge of identifying telomere biology disorders (TBDs) in patients who lack the classical mucocutaneous triad of oral leukoplakia, nail dystrophy, and reticular skin pigmentation that defines dyskeratosis congenita. Using this case as a springboard, we discuss how TBDs can present in adulthood with isolated organ involvement—bone marrow failure, idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis, or hepatic fibrosis—and how these patients are frequently misdiagnosed in non-specialized centers. We review the broader TBD spectrum including Hoyeraal-Hreidarsson, Revesz, and Coats plus syndromes, and offer a practical framework for when to suspect a TBD in a young adult with unexplained multisystem disease. The key takeaway: premature greying, osteoporosis, and cytopenia in a 20-something should trigger genetic evaluation even without the textbook triad.

blogs.title: PARN Mutations: Monoallelic vs. Biallelic and the Expanding Spectrum from Pulmonary Fibrosis to Hepatic Cirrhosis
blogs.description: This post dives into the specific genetics and phenotypic spectrum of PARN mutations. We review how biallelic PARN variants classically cause autosomal recessive dyskeratosis congenita (DKCB6) and Hoyeraal-Hreidarsson syndrome, while monoallelic variants are more commonly associated with telomere-related pulmonary fibrosis and/or bone marrow failure (PFBMFT4). The case under discussion is notable because the patient harbored only a monoallelic PARN variant yet developed both hepatic and pulmonary fibrosis—hepatic fibrosis being a phenotype more classically linked to TERT or TERC mutations. We discuss the concept of haploinsufficiency in PARN (among the 20% of genes least tolerant to rare disruptive variants), the role of incomplete penetrance and environmental factors in variable organ involvement, and how this case expands the recognized clinical spectrum of PARN-associated TBDs.

blogs.title: What Do I Do With a Variant of Uncertain Significance? A Clinician's Guide to ACMG Framework and Clinical-Genetic Correlation
blogs.description: This post tackles the practical challenge of interpreting a Variant of Uncertain Significance (VUS) in clinical practice. The patient's PARN variant (c.613T>C; p.Cys205Arg) was classified as a VUS, yet the clinical team used it to support a TBD diagnosis. We walk through the ACMG/AMP variant classification framework as applied here—PM1 (variant in a critical functional domain, the R3H domain), PM2 (absent from population databases), PP3 (multiple in silico tools predict damaging effect), and PP2 (PARN has a low rate of benign missense variation)—and discuss how clinicians can weigh these supportive criteria alongside the clinical phenotype. We also compare this variant to other PARN missense variants classified as likely pathogenic in ClinVar (p.Lys59Arg, p.Ala383Val) and discuss the tension between waiting for definitive variant classification and acting on clinical suspicion in progressive diseases.

blogs.title: The Disproportionate Cytopenia: When B12 Deficiency Is the Tip of the Iceberg
blogs.description: This post focuses on the diagnostic reasoning when nutritional deficiency doesn't tell the whole story. The patient presented with severe vitamin B12 and folate deficiency, dimorphic anemia, basophilic stippling, Cabot rings, and hypersegmented neutrophils—findings fully consistent with megaloblastic anemia. Yet even after correction of nutritional deficiencies, the systemic dysfunction (pancytopenia, hepatic fibrosis, pulmonary fibrosis, neuropathy, osteoporosis) remained disproportionate and persistent. We discuss the concept of 'disproportionate presentation' as a trigger to look beyond the obvious diagnosis, the role of a positive DAT as a potential distractor, and how underlying telomere shortening may render bone marrow more susceptible to hematopoietic stress such as severe B12 deficiency. The teaching point: correcting a deficiency doesn't exclude a concomitant genetic disorder, and a low reticulocyte response disproportionate to the degree of anemia should prompt further investigation.

blogs.title: The Forgotten Organ: Hepatic Fibrosis in Telomere Biology Disorders and Why You Should Screen for It
blogs.description: This post highlights the underrecognized prevalence of hepatic fibrosis in TBDs. While pulmonary fibrosis and bone marrow failure are well-known complications, hepatic fibrosis has historically been overlooked. We review emerging data from the Aachen Telomere Biology Disease Registry showing that 88.8% of adult patients with pathogenic TERC or TERT mutations had at least moderate hepatic fibrosis and 33.3% had cirrhosis on transient elastography. We discuss the case patient who presented with cirrhosis (liver stiffness 18.1 kPa) without any identifiable infectious, autoimmune, or metabolic cause, and how this finding contributed to the suspicion of a TBD. We also review a comparable published case of a patient with pancytopenia and hepatic fibrosis carrying monoallelic variants in both PARN and TERT. The practical takeaway: transient elastography should be part of routine surveillance in patients with known or suspected TBDs, regardless of the primary genetic variant identified.

blogs.title: Managing Telomere Biology Disorders: Surveillance, Androgens, Transplantation, and the Counseling Conversation
blogs.description: This post covers the management landscape for TBDs, from supportive care to potentially curative options. We discuss the current gold standard for diagnosis (next-generation sequencing plus flow-FISH telomere length measurement), the role of supportive care tailored to organ-specific manifestations, and the indications for hematopoietic stem cell transplantation in patients with progressive bone marrow failure. We review the emerging but still experimental role of androgens (danazol, nandrolone) in telomere elongation, noting that preclinical and small clinical studies are promising but long-term effects remain unknown. We also address the critical importance of genetic counseling for the family given the implications for relatives who may carry the same variant, and the nuanced conversation with patients about the chronic, progressive nature of TBDs when curative options are not feasible. Using the case patient's acceptance of her diagnosis and her ongoing surveillance plan as a model, we discuss how to frame prognosis and set realistic expectations.
